name: Arduino Uno: two LEDs and a button on a breadboard
status: draft layout: BENCH moves holes to match the real breadboard
power: USB from the laptop into the Uno. The Uno's 5V and GND feed the breadboard rails. No battery, no soldering.
rule: LED resistor R = (5 V - vf) / target current, then the nearest value on the rack; keep every pin at or below 20 mA. The button uses a 10 kOhm pull-down so the pin reads LOW until it is pressed.

pins.D2: button to 5 V, R3 pull-down to GND

board.columns: a-e and f-j, split by the centre gap; a + and a - rail on each side
board.coords: row number plus column letter, e.g. b10; rails are '+L', '-L' (left) and '+R', '-R' (right)

prefit.what: jumper, Uno 5V to the left + rail
jumper, Uno GND to the left - rail
jumpers joining left and right rails
5 mm red LED, long leg (anode) in row 14
jumper, red LED cathode row to ground
5 mm blue LED, long leg (anode) in row 24
jumper, blue LED cathode row to ground
6 mm push button across the centre gap
jumper, button top row to 5 V

steps.say: Blue LED on an Arduino pin: 5 minus 3.1 is 1.9 volts. At 13 milliamps that is 150 ohms. Brown, green, brown.
The red LED drops less voltage, so it needs more resistance for the same brightness: 3 volts at 13 milliamps is 220 ohms. Red, red, brown.

steps.what: pull-down for the button on D2
steps.say: The button needs a pull-down so D2 reads LOW until you press it. 10 kilo-ohms: brown, black, orange.

finale: Claude writes the sketch (press the button, the LEDs take turns), compiles and uploads it with arduino-cli (board arduino:avr:uno), then checks through the table camera that both LEDs light.

rack.note: Every value has a different pair of first two bands. 330, 470 and 680 are distractors. Keep 1 kOhm off the rack: it differs from 10 kOhm only in the third band.
